A1-A2.headline: The Ancient Path of Northern Gold

pages.text:
Long ago, a great trade road ran across Europe. It stretched from the cold Baltic Sea to the warm south.

People moved bright yellow amber along this path. Many called this clear tree stone the gold of the north.
pages.caption: The ancient route from the Baltic to the Mediterranean.

evidence.articleCaption: The ancient route from the Baltic Sea to the areas of the Roman Empire by the Mediterranean Sea

pages.text:
This old trade started by the 16th century BC. Traders carried bright amber across rivers, hills, and green valleys for thousands of years.

Old Baltic amber was later found very far away in Egypt and Mycenae. This shows how much early kings and rich people loved the warm color and beauty of the stone.

During Roman times, the road grew even more important. Both traders and Roman soldiers used the same paths to travel across Europe.

Roman leaders built strong walls along the road to keep travelers safe from local attacks. These busy trade paths helped link many different towns and people together.

Modern studies still show how big this trade was. In Wrocław, workers found a huge store of old amber.

The heavy pieces weighed between 1,240 and 1,760 kilograms in total. It proves how active the route once was.
pages.caption: Amber deposits found in different parts of Europe.

B1-B2.headline: Tracing the Ancient Amber Road Across Europe

pages.text:
The Amber Road was an ancient trade network reaching from the cold Baltic coast to the warm Mediterranean. Traders moved fossilized resin known as amber.

Often called the gold of the north, it linked distant regions for ages.
pages.caption: The ancient route from the Baltic to the Mediterranean.

evidence.articleCaption: The ancient route from the Baltic Sea to the areas of the Roman Empire by the Mediterranean Sea

pages.text:
Evidence shows that long-distance amber trade began by the 16th century BC. Merchants transported the glowing material across rivers and mountain passes in Europe.

Experts have recovered Baltic amber as far south as Egypt and Mycenae. That proves how strongly ancient cultures prized its color and rare appeal.

During the Roman era, the corridor served both active commerce and military movement. Soldiers marched north along the same roads that carried rich cargo south.

To protect traveling merchants from local raids, Roman authorities built defensive walls along key stretches. These routes linked diverse European regions.

Modern research continues to reveal the surprising scale of this ancient exchange. In Wrocław, experts uncovered a massive deposit of stored amber.

Estimated between 1,240 and 1,760 kilograms, the find confirms intense trade.
pages.caption: Amber deposits found in different parts of Europe.

C1-C2.headline: The Amber Road: A Conduit of Ancient Continental Exchange

pages.text:
The Amber Road constituted a transcontinental commercial corridor linking frigid Baltic littoral zones with Mediterranean civilizations.

Celebrated as northern gold, fossilized amber sustained interregional exchange across millennia.
pages.caption: The ancient route from the Baltic to the Mediterranean.

evidence.articleCaption: The ancient route from the Baltic Sea to the areas of the Roman Empire by the Mediterranean Sea

pages.text:
Archaeological chronology establishes organized procurement by the 16th century BC, predating classical empires across continental Europe. Artisans valued Baltic resin for its translucence and electrostatic allure.

Specimens excavated in Egypt and Mycenae substantiate expansive prehistoric distribution networks spanning remarkably disparate civilizations.

Under imperial Roman administration, the thoroughfare acquired dual geopolitical significance, facilitating lucrative mercantile caravans alongside rapid legionary deployment across frontier territories.

Authorities erected fortified defensive perimeters to shield vulnerable traders from indigenous incursions, gradually integrating heterogeneous European provinces.

Contemporary excavation persistently illuminates the commercial magnitude of northern amber stockpiling.

In Wrocław, archaeologists documented a colossal subterranean cache estimated between 1,240 and 1,760 kilograms.
